section.title: The Paralytic, Levi, and the Sabbath
section.sectionRationale: Mark gathers a first cluster of controversies. Jesus forgives and heals a paralytic, claiming a right belonging to God alone; He calls a tax collector and eats with sinners; He answers questions about fasting with the joy of the bridegroom; and He declares Himself Lord of the Sabbath. Opposition begins to gather even as the good news widens to the outsider.
section.thesis: The Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins and to reinterpret the Sabbath, and He came not to call the righteous but sinners, so that His arrival is like a wedding feast and a new wine that the old forms cannot contain.
section.frameNote: Five beats: the paralytic forgiven and healed; the call of Levi and the meal with sinners; the question about fasting and the bridegroom; the parables of patch and wineskins; and the Lord of the Sabbath.

units.label: The paralytic forgiven and healed
units.note: the Son of Man has authority to forgive

verses.text: A few days later Jesus went back to Capernaum. And when the people heard that He was home,
they gathered in such large numbers that there was no more room, not even outside the door, as Jesus spoke the word to them.
Then a paralytic was brought to Him, carried by four men.
Since they were unable to get to Jesus through the crowd, they uncovered the roof above Him, made an opening, and lowered the paralytic on his mat.
When Jesus saw their faith, He said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are {{aphiemi|forgiven}}.”
But some of the scribes were sitting there and thinking in their hearts,
“Why does this man speak like this? He is blaspheming! Who can forgive sins but God alone?”
At once Jesus knew in His spirit that they were thinking this way within themselves. “Why are you thinking these things in your hearts?” He asked.
“Which is easier: to say to a paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up, pick up your mat, and walk’?
But so that you may know that the {{huiosanthropou|Son of Man}} has authority on earth to forgive sins...” He said to the paralytic,
“I tell you, get up, pick up your mat, and go home.”
And immediately the man got up, picked up his mat, and walked out in front of them all. As a result, they were all astounded and glorified God, saying, “We have never seen anything like this!”

units.label: The call of Levi and the meal with sinners
units.note: I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners

verses.text: Once again Jesus went out beside the sea. All the people came to Him, and He taught them there.
As He was walking along, He saw Levi son of Alphaeus sitting at the tax booth. “Follow Me,” He told him, and Levi got up and followed Him.
While Jesus was dining at Levi’s house, many tax collectors and {{hamartolos|sinners}} were eating with Him and His disciples, for there were many who followed Him.
When the scribes who were Pharisees saw Jesus eating with these people, they asked His disciples, “Why does He eat with tax collectors and sinners?”
On hearing this, Jesus told them, “It is not the healthy who need a doctor, but the sick. I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners.”

units.label: The question about fasting and the bridegroom
units.note: how can the guests fast while the bridegroom is here

verses.text: Now John’s disciples and the Pharisees were often fasting. So people came to Jesus and asked, “Why don’t Your disciples fast like John’s disciples and those of the Pharisees?”
Jesus replied, “How can the guests of the {{nymphios|bridegroom}} fast while He is with them? As long as He is with them, they cannot fast.
But the time will come when the bridegroom will be taken from them; then they will fast.
No one sews a patch of unshrunk cloth on an old garment. If he does, the new piece will pull away from the old, and a worse tear will result.
And no one pours new wine into old wineskins. If he does, the wine will burst the skins, and both the wine and the wineskins will be ruined. Instead, new wine is poured into new wineskins.”

units.label: The Lord of the Sabbath
units.note: the Sabbath was made for man

verses.text: One Sabbath Jesus was passing through the grainfields, and His disciples began to pick the heads of grain as they walked along.
So the Pharisees said to Him, “Look, why are they doing what is unlawful on the Sabbath?”
Jesus replied, “Have you never read what David did when he and his companions were hungry and in need?
During the high priesthood of Abiathar, he entered the house of God and ate the consecrated bread, which was lawful only for the priests. And he gave some to his companions as well.”
Then Jesus declared, “The {{sabbaton|Sabbath}} was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.
Therefore, the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.”

aphiemi.gloss: To send away, release, forgive. To forgive sins is to remit the debt owed to God, cancelling guilt. The scribes rightly know this is God's prerogative, which is why Jesus' words provoke the charge of blasphemy, and why His healing proves His right to speak them.

huiosanthropou.gloss: Son of Man, Jesus' favourite self-designation in Mark. It draws on Daniel 7:13-14, where one like a son of man is given everlasting dominion by God. The title holds together true humanity and divine authority, here the authority on earth to forgive sins.

hamartolos.gloss: A sinner, one outside the bounds of the law-keeping community, morally and socially disreputable. Jesus deliberately shares table with such people, declaring that He came precisely to call sinners, not those who reckon themselves righteous.

nymphios.gloss: Bridegroom. In the Old Testament the LORD is the husband of His people; Jesus takes the title for Himself, so His presence is a wedding celebration. The hint that the bridegroom will be taken away is the first quiet foreshadowing of the cross.

sabbaton.gloss: The Sabbath, the seventh-day rest commanded in the law as a gift to humanity. Jesus insists the Sabbath was made to serve people, not to enslave them, and claims to be its Lord, the one with authority to say what the day truly means.

basic.context: Mark lines up five scenes where Jesus collides with the religious leaders. Four friends dig through a roof to lower a paralyzed man to Jesus, who forgives his sins, then heals him to prove He has the right to forgive. He calls Levi, a despised tax collector, and shares a meal with tax collectors and sinners, saying He came for the sick, not the self-satisfied. Asked why His disciples do not fast, He says you cannot fast at a wedding while the bridegroom is present. His newness cannot be patched onto the old system. And He declares Himself Lord of the Sabbath.
basic.hermeneutics: Read these as a series building one case: Jesus claims prerogatives that belong to God. He forgives sins, welcomes sinners, calls Himself the bridegroom of God's people, and reinterprets the Sabbath as its Lord. The opposition that begins here will grow until it turns deadly. The healing is offered as visible proof of an invisible reality, forgiveness.
basic.originalLanguages: Jesus tells the paralytic his sins are aphiemi, forgiven, a word for the release of a debt only God can grant. He calls Himself the huiosanthropou, the Son of Man of Daniel 7, with authority on earth to forgive. He came to call hamartolos, sinners. He is the nymphios, the bridegroom, whose presence is joy. And He is Lord of the sabbaton, the Sabbath.
basic.typology: David eating the consecrated bread foreshadows the greater Son of David who has authority over the holy things. The bridegroom imagery, drawn from the prophets who called the LORD Israel's husband, points to Jesus as the divine bridegroom. The new wine and new cloth signal the new covenant breaking in.
basic.christ: Jesus does what only God can do: He forgives sins. He calls Himself the Son of Man with divine authority, the bridegroom of God's people, and the Lord of the Sabbath. His words and works together announce that God Himself has come to save sinners.
basic.god: Only God can forgive sins, the scribes say, and they are right, which is exactly the point. In Jesus, God draws near to forgive, to welcome sinners to His table, and to give His people rest. God's holiness and His mercy meet in the Son of Man.
basic.crossReferences: Daniel 7 gives the Son of Man his dominion. 1 Samuel 21 tells of David and the consecrated bread. Isaiah 62 and Hosea 2 present the LORD as bridegroom, fulfilled in Christ.
basic.oneStory: God had promised to forgive His people's sins, to feast with them, and to give them rest. In Jesus all of this arrives. He forgives, He gathers sinners to the wedding table, and He is Lord of the Sabbath rest. The old forms cannot contain the new thing God is doing; the kingdom has come in the Son of Man.

context.literary:
Mark 2:1 to 3:6 is a single block of five conflict stories, and chapter 2 contains the first four. Scholars have long noticed that Mark arranged them in a deliberate order, since the first and last are both about authority claimed by the Son of Man, and the thread of the leaders' growing hostility climbs from a silent accusation in the heart, 2:6, to a spoken complaint to the disciples, 2:16, to a direct challenge to Jesus, 2:24, and finally to a plot to destroy Him in 3:6. The reader sees a hostility that starts in the mind and ends in a conspiracy.

Inside the block the pairs are matched. The first story begins with a house and a roof and ends with the crowd glorifying God. The call of Levi and the dinner follow, and both include a saying of Jesus that explains His mission, 'I have not come to call the righteous, but sinners', verse 17. Then two sayings about fasting and new things set Jesus' coming in the image of a wedding feast and fresh cloth and wine. The final story, in the grainfields, returns to a question of what is lawful and ends with another claim of lordship. The central sayings in verses 17, 19 to 22 and 27 to 28 are all short, memorable, and in the form of proverb or parable.

Mark also uses a literary device of interruption. In the paralytic story, the declaration of forgiveness is followed by a pause in which the scribes reason in their hearts, and then Jesus' words to them break into the sentence of verse 10, where the phrase 'But so that you may know' is left unfinished and Jesus turns to the paralytic. The grammar of the sentence stumbles because the real subject of the scene is not the healing but the claim that lies behind it. The chapter ends with the title 'Lord', the highest claim of all.
context.historical:
Capernaum houses of that period were modest dwellings of local basalt stone with flat roofs made of beams, branches and packed earth, often reached by an outside stair. That explains how four men could carry a man up and dig through the roof, verse 4, and why the owner of the house, probably Simon, Mark 1:29, did not have a ceiling to break but a covering that could be removed and repaired. The mat on which the paralytic was lowered was a poor man's bed, and the home where Jesus taught was filled to the doorway.

Tax collectors were widely despised. They worked under contract for the Roman government or its client rulers and collected more than was due to profit themselves. A tax collector sat at a toll point and taxed goods in transit, and this one was on the road by the sea at Capernaum, in the territory of Herod Antipas. In the eyes of the pious, such men were collaborators with Rome and often cheats, and the phrase 'tax collectors and sinners' in verses 15 and 16 describes people who were excluded from respectable company. Table fellowship carried meaning. To eat with someone was to accept them, and for the Pharisees, whose practice was to keep purity at the table, it was scandalous that Jesus shared meals with those who were considered unclean.

Fasting was a regular practice among the pious. The Law required fasting on the Day of Atonement, and the prophets had added days of mourning, Zechariah 8:19. Pharisees fasted voluntarily, Luke 18:12, and John's disciples took up the practice as part of their call to repentance. A wedding in the village was a week of festivity, and the guests of the bridegroom would be excused from fasting. Finally, Sabbath observance, based on Exodus 20:8 to 11, was one of the defining marks of Jewish identity. By the first century it had acquired a body of detailed rules about what counted as work, and picking and rubbing grain was regarded by strict teachers as a form of reaping, although the Law itself allowed plucking grain from a neighbor's field, Deuteronomy 23:25.
context.canonical:
The claim to forgive sins rests on one of the deepest convictions of the Old Testament, that forgiveness belongs to God alone. God proclaimed Himself to Moses as 'forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin', Exodus 34:7, and the Psalms and prophets repeat it. 'I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake', Isaiah 43:25. The scribes' reaction in verse 7 is therefore a theological reaction and not mere pettiness. By the standard of the Law, a man who claimed to forgive sins was claiming the prerogative of God. The story leaves the reader with the choice that Mark intends: either Jesus is a blasphemer, or God has come near in Him.

The title Son of Man comes from Daniel 7:13 to 14, where one like a son of man receives dominion from the Ancient of Days. Jesus uses it of Himself in verse 10 and again in verse 28, both times with a claim of authority. The image of the bridegroom comes from the prophets who speak of the LORD as husband to His people, Isaiah 54:5, Isaiah 62:5, Hosea 2:16 and Jeremiah 31:32. In Hosea 2:19 to 20 He promises to betroth Israel to Himself forever. Jesus' use of the image without comment assumes the role of the divine husband. The New Testament will pick it up in John 3:29, 2 Corinthians 11:2, Ephesians 5:25 to 27 and Revelation 19:7.

The controversy over the Sabbath looks back to the creation account, where God rested on the seventh day and blessed it, Genesis 2:2 to 3, to the law of Exodus 20:8 to 11, and to Deuteronomy 5:14 to 15 with its note that servants and the foreigner should rest too. Jesus draws on 1 Samuel 21 and on Hosea 6:6, which Matthew's parallel quotes, Matthew 12:7. Later Scripture discusses the Sabbath as a shadow of what is to come, Colossians 2:16 to 17, and as a rest that remains for the people of God, Hebrews 4:9 to 10.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Mark arranged these stories to show that Jesus' claims are the source of the conflict, not a side effect. In each of the four scenes Jesus says or does something that sets Him in the place of God, and each time He is challenged and answers with a saying that explains it. The paralytic story is the most striking, since Jesus lets the accusation of blasphemy stand until He has proved by a visible healing that He has the authority He claims. Mark wants his readers to think hard about whether what Jesus says is true, and he leaves them with an argument in the form of an event.

The second purpose is to show who Jesus came for. 'Not the righteous, but sinners' is a statement of mission, and the stories show it in practice: He forgives a paralytic, He calls a tax collector, and He eats with the outcast. The scribes' complaint that He eats with sinners is Mark's way of showing the offense of grace.

The third purpose is to prepare the readers for the old and the new. The sayings about the bridegroom, the cloth and the wine tell them that something new has come that cannot be added to the old forms without breaking either. Mark's Christian readers, probably a mix of Jews and Gentiles, needed to understand why the old patterns of observance no longer governed their life, and the Sabbath controversy answers that question from the lips of Jesus.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The stories describe the conflict between Jesus and the leaders of His day and do not give a rule for each case. The fact that Jesus ate with sinners does not mean believers must ignore holiness, and the fact that David ate the consecrated bread does not mean that anyone may break the commands of God when hungry. Jesus makes a particular point about what David did and what the Sabbath is for, and He does not offer a general license.

What clearly carries forward is the character of His mission and the manner of His welcome. His followers are meant to share meals with people the respectable avoid, to bring the helpless to Him as the four friends did, and to measure religion by mercy and not by status. The saying that the Sabbath was made for man tells us how to read rest: as a gift. The church has differed on how Christians should keep a day of rest, and Paul is careful to say that each person should be fully convinced in his own mind, Romans 14:5. The text itself does not specify a Christian pattern of Sabbath observance, so it should not be used as a rule on either side. The fasting saying is also descriptive: Jesus says His disciples will fast when the bridegroom is taken away, and the church has treated that as a permission and not a duty to fast on particular days.

debates.question: Does Mark's reference to Abiathar contradict 1 Samuel 21?

views.label: Mark is imprecise, or the name is a loose reference
views.case: In 1 Samuel 21:1 to 6 it is Ahimelech who gives David the consecrated bread, and Abiathar is Ahimelech's son who escaped and joined David, 1 Samuel 22:20. Some say Mark names the better known priest of David's reign by mistake, or that a copyist's change entered the text. Matthew and Luke do not repeat the name, which suggests they noticed the difficulty.

views.label: The phrase marks the time or the larger story
views.case: Others argue that 'during the high priesthood of Abiathar' may be read as 'in the passage about Abiathar', as the Jews would refer to a section of Scripture by its prominent figure, or that the phrase refers to the period in which Abiathar was prominent. Others note that father and son are sometimes confused in the books of Samuel and Chronicles, as in 2 Samuel 8:17 and 1 Chronicles 24:6, which speak of Ahimelech son of Abiathar, and that Abiathar was in any case the priest most closely tied to David.

debates.bearing: The difficulty is real and Christians have long handled it in more than one way. None of the explanations affects the argument Jesus makes, which rests on what David did and not on the name of the priest. A reader may hold the question loosely and still follow the point: if a hungry David could be allowed the holy bread, the Son of David and Lord of the Sabbath is free to let His hungry disciples eat.

debates.question: What does 'Son of Man' mean in verses 10 and 28?

views.label: A title from Daniel 7
views.case: Jesus draws on Daniel 7:13 to 14, in which a figure like a son of man receives dominion, glory and kingship from the Ancient of Days. The setting of the claim, authority over sin and over the Sabbath, fits that exalted background, and Jesus applies the title to Himself in Mark 14:62 when He answers the high priest.

views.label: A reference to humanity in general
views.case: The phrase 'son of man' can simply mean a human being, as in Psalm 8 and throughout Ezekiel. Some say that in verse 28 it means that human beings have authority over the Sabbath, since verse 27 says it was made for man. Mark's wording in verse 28, 'Therefore', links the two verses closely.

debates.bearing: The two readings are not far apart. Jesus is the representative man and the divine figure of Daniel at once. His authority over sin is not something every person has, as verse 10 makes clear, and the authority over the Sabbath is given in the person of the Son of Man. The wider Gospel shows that the title is used of One who has authority and also suffers, Mark 8:31 and 10:45.

debates.question: Did Jesus abolish the Sabbath?

views.label: He fulfilled and reinterpreted it
views.case: Jesus does not say the Sabbath is abolished. He says it was made for man and that He is Lord of it. In Matthew's parallel He adds that the priests in the temple break the Sabbath and are innocent, and that something greater than the temple is here, Matthew 12:5 to 6. The Sabbath is given its true purpose and its Lord.

views.label: He set aside its binding force for the new age
views.case: Others stress the pattern of new cloth and new wine, and Paul's statement that the Sabbath is a shadow of things to come and the body belongs to Christ, Colossians 2:16 to 17. They see in Mark 2 the start of a shift in which the Sabbath's place is taken by the rest that comes in Christ, Hebrews 4:9 to 10.

debates.bearing: All agree that Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath and that its purpose is the good of people under God. They differ on how a Christian should keep a day of rest. The text of Mark does not settle that, so it is wise to honour both its generosity and its authority and to avoid using it as a weapon against others who read it differently.

study.originalLanguages:
The four friends' effort is told in a series of vivid verbs. They 'uncovered the roof', apestegasan ten stegen, which means they unroofed it, and then exoruxantes, 'having dug out', the opening. The word krabattos for the paralytic's 'mat' is a plain, everyday word for a simple bed, and Mark keeps it through the story, so that in verse 11 Jesus' command to 'pick up your mat' uses the same humble word. Then Jesus addresses the man with teknon, 'child', a word of tenderness that tells us the man was not a case to Jesus but someone He cared for. He does not say 'be healed' but 'your sins are forgiven', and the declaration is made in the plainest terms. Aphiemi, 'forgive', is the same verb that Mark has already used of the disciples who 'left' their nets, as in Mark 1:18, and it carries the sense of letting go and sending away.

The scribes are 'reasoning', dialogizomenoi, in their hearts. The word suggests argument within the mind and not just a passing thought, and Jesus perceives it 'in His spirit'. Their charge is that He blasphemes, the verb blasphemeo, which means to speak against God's honour. The question 'Which is easier?' uses eukopoteron, a comparative that means easier or less laborious. To say 'your sins are forgiven' costs nothing to speak, and no one can check it, while to say 'get up and walk' can be seen at once. Jesus does the harder thing in public to prove the one that cannot be seen. And His word to the man, egeire, 'rise', is the verb of resurrection used of Peter's mother-in-law in Mark 1:31 and of Jesus Himself in Mark 16:6.

Levi's call uses the language of Mark 1:17. 'Follow Me' is a present imperative, akolouthei moi, which suggests a continuing following, and Levi 'got up', the same verb, and followed. The tax booth is the telonion, the customs post, and a telones was a collector of tolls. The saying of verse 17 turns on two Greek words. The 'sick' are those kakos echontes, literally 'those who have it badly', and the physician is the iatros. The 'righteous', dikaious, are those who count themselves righteous. Jesus' irony is mild and sharp: He comes to call those who know they need Him.

The wedding image is more exact in Greek. The guests are literally 'the sons of the bridechamber', hoi huioi tou nymphonos, a Semitic way to describe the wedding party. The phrase shows that Jesus is thinking of the week-long feast. The cloth is agnaphos, 'unshrunk', and the new wine is oinos neos, using neos, which suggests wine that is young and still fermenting. The skins at the end are said to be kainous, 'fresh' or 'new', a different word that stresses quality. Jesus does not tell people to patch up the old but to receive something that is both young and of a new kind.

The Sabbath dispute turns on exestin, 'it is lawful', a word that appears again at 3:4. The disciples' act is described as 'making a way' while plucking, and the complaint is that they are doing 'what is not lawful'. Jesus' reply is that the Sabbath 'came to be', egeneto, 'for the sake of man', dia ton anthropon, and not man for the Sabbath. The verb is the verb of creation, and it points back to the original gift of the day. The phrase translated 'consecrated bread' is literally 'the loaves of the presentation', tous artous tes protheseos, as the footnote says 'the Bread of the Presence'. It was the twelve loaves set out in the sanctuary each Sabbath, Leviticus 24:5 to 9, and this is the bread David took.

typology.type: David and the bread of the Presence, 1 Samuel 21
typology.fulfillment: David, anointed but not yet enthroned, was hungry and fugitive, and the priest gave him the consecrated bread because there was nothing else, 1 Samuel 21:4 to 6. Jesus uses the story to argue that human need and the status of the one in need can take priority over ritual limits. David was the anointed king in waiting, and Jesus is the greater Son of David, rejected and followed by hungry companions. The correspondence is of situation and person. The escalation is that David was a king by promise who had to take what was not his, while Jesus is Lord of the Sabbath in His own right. The type falls short because David's act was a rare exception, whereas Jesus claims a standing authority.

The prophets used marriage as the picture of God's covenant with Israel. The LORD is Israel's husband, Isaiah 54:5, and He will rejoice over her as a bridegroom over his bride, Isaiah 62:5. Jesus takes this image and applies it to Himself, in Mark 2:19 to 20, without explanation. His presence is the wedding, and the feast has begun. The New Testament develops the picture, so that Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her, Ephesians 5:25, and the marriage supper of the Lamb is the final feast, Revelation 19:7 to 9. The image falls short only in that the bridegroom 'will be taken from them', a sign of the cross, which no earthly wedding has.

The prophets promised a day when the mountains would drip with sweet wine, Amos 9:13, and a feast of choice wine for all peoples, Isaiah 25:6. Jeremiah foretold a new covenant unlike the old, Jeremiah 31:31 to 34. Jesus' saying about new wine says that the new covenant cannot simply be poured into the old arrangements. In His death He would speak of the fruit of the vine drunk anew in the kingdom, Mark 14:25. It is an image and not a mechanical type, and it should not be pressed to mean that the old covenant was worthless; Hebrews says it was made obsolete by a better one, Hebrews 8:13, and the old was good for its purpose.

God rested on the seventh day and blessed it, Genesis 2:2 to 3, and Israel was told to keep the Sabbath as a sign between God and themselves, Ezekiel 20:12. The day looked back to creation and, in Deuteronomy 5:15, to the rescue from slavery in Egypt. Jesus as Lord of the Sabbath is the one in whom the rest is found, and Hebrews says that 'there remains, then, a Sabbath rest for the people of God', Hebrews 4:9. In Matthew He says, 'Come to Me, all you who are weary', in Matthew 11:28. The weekly day was a sign that pointed to the rest that Christ brings, and the sign continues to teach even as the reality has come.

study.christ:
Everything in Mark 2 is a claim about Jesus, and the claims go as high as claims can go. In the first scene He does what the scribes rightly say only God can do. Mark does not soften the claim: the scribes say, 'Who can forgive sins but God alone?' and Jesus does not correct them. He takes their premise and shows by His next act that it applies to Him. The healing is the evidence of the unseen forgiveness. He knows what they are thinking in their hearts, which is another divine ability, as 1 Kings 8:39 says that God alone knows the hearts of men.

He is the Son of Man who has authority on earth. The title comes from Daniel 7, where it names the figure who receives everlasting dominion, and Jesus here uses it twice, once of the right to forgive and once of the right over the Sabbath. Notice 'on earth', verse 10. The scribes think of forgiveness as something that happens in heaven. Jesus says that the Son of Man has the authority here and now to say it. The kingdom has come near, and the King pronounces forgiveness from within it.

He is the physician for sinners. When He says that He has come to call sinners, He gives a short account of His mission and does not hide the offence of it. The good news is for those who know they are sick, and Levi's feast is a picture of the welcome. The theme will deepen until Mark 10:45, where He gives His life as a ransom for many. The doctor does not simply visit the sick; He takes their sickness. And since He is among sinners as the sinless One, He is holy company who does not lose His holiness by contact, as with the leper in chapter 1.

He is the bridegroom. In the Old Testament this is the role of the LORD. The bridegroom's presence makes fasting out of place, and then He says that He will be taken away. In a Gospel that is heading toward the cross, that is the first hint of His death, and Mark places it in a wedding saying so that the reader notes how joy and loss are linked. Christ is the one whose presence is the feast, and whose absence will bring a time of mourning that is then ended in the resurrection.

He is Lord of the Sabbath. The Sabbath was God's own day, and to call oneself its Lord is to claim the place of God. Yet Jesus does it in the language of care, 'the Sabbath was made for man', so His lordship is of a king who serves. The link to David is the link to a rightful but unrecognized king. We should be careful not to read too much into details such as the number of friends or the roof. The links to Christ lie in the claims He makes and the works that back them.
study.god:
The scribes in this chapter are right about something important: only God can forgive sins. That sentence stands in the text uncorrected and is the starting point for what Mark shows about God. God is the one against whom sin is committed and the one who has authority to pardon. The Old Testament makes forgiveness part of His self-revelation, 'compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion and faithfulness ... forgiving iniquity, transgression, and sin', Exodus 34:6 to 7. The man on the mat is given exactly that.

The chapter shows God as one who takes the initiative to forgive before being asked. The paralytic did not ask for forgiveness. Jesus saw the faith of the friends and spoke first to the deeper need. The man came for his legs, and was given what he needed more. God's concern goes beyond the visible problem. He heals the body as a sign, but He begins with the cause of separation.

It shows God's holiness and God's welcome belonging together. The scribes assume that holiness means separation from sinners. In Jesus, holiness comes close, eats with them, and is not tainted. This is consistent with God's character in the Old Testament, who 'delights in loving devotion', Micah 7:18, and who 'will cast out all our sins into the depths of the sea', Micah 7:19. Hosea's saying, 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice', Hosea 6:6, which Matthew's parallel records at Matthew 9:13, shows that this was always the heart of God. The Pharisees knew the commands, and Jesus' defence of table fellowship shows what the commands were for.

It shows God as the giver of rest. In Genesis God rested, and in Exodus and Deuteronomy He gave His people a day to rest and remember. The statement that the Sabbath was made for man shows a God who gives gifts for the benefit of His creatures and not a heavenly rule-maker looking for transgressors. The Sabbath was always a mercy, and the God of the Sabbath is the God who works for the good of those He made, as John 5:17 records Jesus saying, 'My Father is at His work, and I too am working.'

It shows God as faithful to a plan that is still moving. The new wine requires new wineskins because God is doing something new in the fulfilment of His promises. He does not discard the old, but He does not bind the new to it. And the sorrow within the wedding, the bridegroom taken away, shows that the plan includes the cross.

For worship, the passage invites us to receive forgiveness as the paralytic did, passively and with astonishment, and to glorify God as the crowd did, saying they had never seen anything like it. It warns us also that those who are most at home in religious life can be the last to see God at work among them.

crossReferences.note: God declares Himself to Moses as compassionate and gracious, forgiving iniquity, transgression and sin. It is the background to the scribes' conviction that only God forgives, and it makes Jesus' pronouncement to the paralytic a claim to act as the God who revealed His name on Sinai.

God says, 'I, yes I, am He who blots out your transgressions for My own sake and remembers your sins no more.' The repetition of 'I' stresses that forgiveness is God's own work. The scribes' question in Mark 2:7 is a faithful echo of this claim.

One like the Son of Man is given dominion by the Ancient of Days. Jesus' use of the title with authority over sin and the Sabbath draws on this vision and presents Himself as the figure who receives and exercises divine rule.

God says, 'I desire mercy, not sacrifice, and the knowledge of God rather than burnt offerings.' Matthew's parallel to the meal with sinners quotes it, Matthew 9:13. It sets the heart of the law as mercy and shows why Jesus can sit with sinners without compromise.

As a bridegroom rejoices over his bride, so God will rejoice over His people. Jesus' saying about the bridegroom in Mark 2:19 draws on the prophets' marriage imagery and applies it to Himself, so that His presence is the joy of God over His people.

David, hungry, receives the consecrated bread from the priest at Nob. Jesus cites the story to answer the Pharisees. The comparison puts David's need above ritual restriction, and it quietly sets Jesus as the greater Son of David.

Twelve loaves were set before the LORD every Sabbath, and only Aaron and his sons were to eat them in a holy place. This is the bread David took and is the law Jesus refers to when He says it was lawful only for the priests.

The commandment to remember the Sabbath and keep it holy, rooted in God's rest at creation. It is the law the Pharisees believed the disciples broke, and the passage Jesus interprets when He says the Sabbath was made for man.

The Sabbath is given so that servants and the foreigner may rest as well, and the people are to remember their slavery in Egypt. It shows that the day was a gift of rescue and rest for the weak, which fits Jesus' statement that it was made for man.

There remains a Sabbath rest for God's people, and whoever enters it rests from his own work. The writer treats the Sabbath as a pointer to the rest found in Christ, so the Lord of the Sabbath of Mark 2:28 is also the giver of its true fulfilment.

Jesus says He will not drink the fruit of the vine until He drinks it anew in the kingdom of God. It links the wedding and wine imagery of Mark 2:19 to 22 to the cross and to the final feast, so that the joy of the bridegroom is promised again after His being taken away.

study.oneStory:
From the garden onward, the human problem has been sin and the separation it brings, and the story of the Bible is the story of how God deals with it. Adam and Eve hid from Him, Genesis 3:8. Israel's law and sacrifices taught that sin was serious and that God was holy, while the prophets promised a day when He would pardon fully. Isaiah heard God say that He would blot out transgressions, and Jeremiah heard of a new covenant in which He would 'forgive their iniquities and will remember their sins no more', Jeremiah 31:34. The long question was how a holy God could do this.

Mark 2 answers by showing that the day has come. In a crowded house in Capernaum a man is told, 'Your sins are forgiven', by the One who stands in the place of God. Nothing in the story is yet said about the cross, but the reader of the whole Gospel knows that this forgiveness will be bought at the cost of the Forgiver. The tax collector's feast shows who is invited to the new community, and the saying about the bridegroom reveals the pain at the heart of the feast. The old wineskins cannot hold what God is now doing, and the story requires a new covenant.

The Sabbath controversy ties into the beginning of the Bible. God rested after His work of creation, and a day of rest was given to a people just freed from slavery. Jesus' claim to be its Lord shows that the one who made the world and gave the rest has come among His people. His disciples pick grain in a field because they are hungry, and the Lord of the Sabbath is providing for them as He had in the wilderness, Exodus 16:23. The final rest, which the Sabbath pointed to, is the rest of the new creation.

The passage sets up what comes next in the Gospel. The opposition that begins in the scribes' hearts becomes a plot by 3:6, and the bridegroom will be taken away. The authority to forgive is exercised in fullness at the cross and the resurrection, and the apostles proclaim that through Jesus forgiveness of sins is announced, Acts 13:38. The church is now the company at the table, and every meal of bread and wine looks back to the one who ate with sinners and forward to the feast.

The story ends in the wedding supper of the Lamb, where the bride has made herself ready and the invited are blessed, Revelation 19:7 to 9. Those who were called sinners and found to be forgiven will sit at that table, and the bridegroom will no longer be taken away. The first scene of forgiveness in Capernaum is a foretaste of a world where nothing separates God and His people, Revelation 21:3 to 4.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus first say to the paralytic, your sins are forgiven, before healing him?

options.text: To meet the man's deepest need and to display His divine authority to forgive, which the healing then proves.
options.note: Jesus makes forgiveness the point and heals to show the Son of Man's authority to forgive, Mark 2:10.

options.text: Because forgiveness was easier to say than to heal.
options.note: Jesus does note it is easy to say, but His aim was to prove that the unseen forgiveness was real, not merely easy words.

options.text: Because the man had asked to be forgiven rather than healed.
options.note: The text does not record such a request; Jesus took the initiative to address sin first.

options.text: Because sin and paralysis are always directly linked.
options.note: Jesus does not teach that this man's paralysis was caused by a specific sin; He addresses the universal need of forgiveness.

quiz.q: Why did the scribes accuse Jesus of blasphemy?

options.text: Because He claimed to forgive sins, which they knew only God can do.
options.note: Mark 2:7, who can forgive sins but God alone; they rightly saw a divine claim.

options.text: Because He healed on the wrong day.
options.note: That charge arises elsewhere; here the offence was specifically His claim to forgive sins.

options.text: Because He touched an unclean person.
options.note: That was an issue with the leper, not the paralytic; the blasphemy charge concerned forgiving sins.

options.text: Because He refused to heal the man.
options.note: Jesus did heal him; the offence was His claim to forgive.

quiz.q: What did Jesus mean by saying He came to call not the righteous but sinners?

options.text: He came to save those who know they are sinners in need of mercy, like the sick who need a doctor.
options.note: Mark 2:17 gives the doctor and the sick as His own explanation.

options.text: He preferred the company of disreputable people to respectable ones.
options.note: He did eat with sinners, but the point is their need of a Saviour, not a mere preference for their company.

options.text: There are some genuinely righteous people who do not need Him.
options.note: The self-styled righteous also need Him; the irony is that they will not admit their sickness.

options.text: He came only for the outwardly moral and religious.
options.note: The opposite: He came for sinners, not the self-satisfied righteous.

quiz.q: Why did Jesus say His disciples do not fast now?

options.text: Because the bridegroom is present, and guests cannot fast at a wedding; they will fast when He is taken away.
options.note: Mark 2:19-20 gives the bridegroom image and the hint of His being taken away.

options.text: Because fasting is no longer a valid practice for anyone.
options.note: Jesus says they will fast when the bridegroom is taken; He does not abolish fasting outright.

options.text: Because His disciples were not spiritual enough to fast.
options.note: It was the joy of the bridegroom's presence, not a lack of devotion, that made fasting unfitting then.

options.text: Because fasting was invented by the Pharisees.
options.note: Fasting was a genuine biblical practice; Jesus addresses its fitting time, not its origin.

quiz.q: What did Jesus claim about the Sabbath?

options.text: The Sabbath was made for man's good, and the Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath.
options.note: Mark 2:27-28 gives both truths together.

options.text: The Sabbath was made for man's good and should be kept flexibly.
options.note: True as far as it goes, but it omits Jesus' central claim to be Lord of the Sabbath.

options.text: The Sabbath no longer matters at all.
options.note: Jesus honours the Sabbath as God's gift; He claims lordship over it rather than dismissing it.

options.text: People exist to serve the Sabbath's rules.
options.note: Jesus says the reverse: the Sabbath was made for man, not man for the Sabbath.

questions: Four friends went to great lengths to bring their paralyzed friend to Jesus. Who in your life needs you to carry them, persistently, to Christ?
Jesus addressed the man's deepest need, forgiveness, before his obvious one. What is the deeper need beneath the things you most often ask God to fix?
Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners and was criticized for it. How does His welcome of sinners shape whom you are willing to draw near to?
The self-styled righteous missed their need of a doctor. Where might you be trusting your own respectability rather than owning your need of mercy?
Jesus is Lord even of the Sabbath and offers true rest. How could you receive the Sabbath as a gift for your good rather than a burden or an afterthought?

translationNotes.note: The sentence breaks off mid-thought in the Greek as Jesus turns from the scribes to the paralytic.

During the high priesthood of Abiathar has occasioned much discussion, since 1 Samuel 21 names Ahimelech; the phrase likely means in the days of Abiathar, a well-known figure of that priestly period, or in the section of Scripture associated with him.
Some manuscripts omit the closing line, new wine is poured into new wineskins; the well-attested reading includes it, sealing the point that the new age needs new forms.
